theorems_and_key_concepts: Force is a push or pull upon an object resulting from its interaction with another object.
Forces are due to an interaction: at least two objects must interact for a force to come into play.
Forces applied in the same direction add up; forces in opposite directions result in net difference.
Force can change the state of motion (speed and direction) and can change the shape of an object.
Contact forces: Muscular force, Friction, Normal force, Tension.
Non-contact forces: Magnetic force, Electrostatic force, Gravitational force.
Pressure is force per unit area. Atmospheric pressure is exerted by the envelope of air surrounding Earth.
learning_outcomes: Identify contact and non-contact forces in daily life.
Calculate pressure given force and contact area.
Demonstrate that liquids and gases exert pressure on the walls of containers.

activities.title: Demonstrating Atmospheric Pressure with a Rubber Sucker
activities.aim: To demonstrate the existence and enormous magnitude of atmospheric pressure using a rubber sucker.
apparatus: Smooth clean flat glass plate or tiled wall
procedure: Take a good quality rubber sucker and press it firmly against a smooth, flat glass plate.
Observe that most of the air trapped between the sucker and the flat surface escapes.
Try pulling the rubber sucker straight off the surface using your hand.
precautions: Ensure the glass plate surface is smooth, clean, and free of dust.
Press evenly so that maximum air is evacuated from underneath the sucker.
activities.observations: The rubber sucker sticks tenaciously to the surface and requires an immense pulling force to detach.
activities.conclusion: Atmospheric pressure acting from the outside presses the sucker firmly against the surface, demonstrating that atmosphere exerts huge pressure.

activities.title: Variation of Liquid Pressure with Depth
activities.aim: To observe that pressure exerted by liquids increases with increasing depth.
apparatus: Tall transparent plastic cylinder or bottle
procedure: Punch three small holes along a vertical line at different heights in the cylinder.
Cover the holes with adhesive tape and fill the cylinder with water.
Remove the tape quickly and observe the jets of water shooting out from the three holes.
precautions: Holes must be of identical diameter.
Maintain a constant water level by slowly pouring water if needed.
activities.observations: Water from the bottom-most hole travels the greatest horizontal distance, while water from the top hole falls closest to the cylinder.
activities.conclusion: Liquid pressure increases with depth below the free surface of the liquid.

theorems_and_key_concepts: Friction is the opposing force that comes into play when two surfaces in contact slide or tend to slide across each other.
Friction always opposes the relative motion between the surfaces in contact.
Friction is caused by the interlocking of microscopic irregularities on the two surfaces.
Factors affecting friction: nature of surfaces and the normal force pressing the surfaces together.
Static friction, sliding friction, and rolling friction: Static > Sliding > Rolling.
Friction is a necessary evil: allows walking, writing, braking, but causes wear and tear and energy loss.
Methods of increasing friction (treads on tyres, spikes on shoes) and decreasing friction (lubricants, ball bearings).
learning_outcomes: Compare static, sliding, and rolling friction.
Identify advantages and disadvantages of friction.
Demonstrate use of ball bearings to convert sliding friction into rolling friction.

activities.title: Comparing Sliding and Rolling Friction
activities.aim: To verify that rolling friction is significantly less than sliding friction.
apparatus: Set of cylindrical pencils or rollers
procedure: Place a thick heavy book on a horizontal table and tie a string around it.
Pull the book across the table with a spring balance and record the reading (sliding friction).
Now place 3 to 4 round pencils underneath the book parallel to each other.
Pull the book again gently and record the spring balance reading as it rolls.
precautions: Pull steadily and horizontally at uniform speed.
Ensure the pencils are round and smooth.
activities.observations: The spring balance reading while rolling over pencils is much smaller than when sliding directly on the tabletop.
activities.conclusion: Rolling friction is substantially smaller than sliding friction, which is why ball bearings and wheels are used.

theorems_and_key_concepts: Natural resources: Inexhaustible (Sunlight, Air) and Exhaustible (Fossil fuels, Forests).
Fossil fuels are formed from the dead remains of living organisms buried millions of years ago.
Coal: Carbonisation process; Products of coal: Coke, Coal tar, Coal gas.
Petroleum: Origin from sea organisms, drilling of crude oil, refining (fractional distillation).
Petroleum fractions: Petroleum gas (LPG), Petrol, Kerosene, Diesel, Lubricating oil, Paraffin wax, Bitumen.
Natural gas: Clean burning fuel stored under high pressure as Compressed Natural Gas (CNG).
Environmental impacts of fossil fuels and PCRA guidelines for fuel conservation.
learning_outcomes: Explain the carbonisation process in coal formation.
List products obtained from fractional distillation of petroleum and their uses.
Suggest conservation practices to reduce fossil fuel consumption.
key_formulas_and_equations: \text{Dead Vegetation} \xrightarrow[\text{Millions of Years}]{\text{High Temp, High Pressure}} \text{Coal} \quad (\text{Carbonisation})

activities.title: Demonstration of Destructive Distillation of Coal
activities.aim: To observe the thermal decomposition of powdered coal in the absence of air.
procedure: Take crushed coal in a hard glass boiling tube and fit a cork with a delivery tube.
Heat the tube strongly over a Bunsen burner flame.
Pass the evolved vapours through water and test the emerging gas with a flame.
precautions: Use a hard borosilicate boiling tube.
Ensure the apparatus is airtight.
activities.observations: A black porous residue (coke) remains in the tube; a thick black liquid (coal tar) condenses in water, and flammable coal gas burns at the jet.
activities.conclusion: Destructive distillation of coal yields coke, coal tar, and coal gas.

theorems_and_key_concepts: A synthetic fibre is a chain of small units (monomers) joined together to form a polymer.
Rayon (artificial silk): prepared from chemical treatment of wood pulp.
Nylon: first fully synthetic fibre made without natural raw material (coal, water, air); strong, elastic, light.
Polyester and Acrylic: Terylene, PET bottles, acrylic (artificial wool).
Characteristics of synthetic fibres: high tensile strength, quick drying, durable, affordable.
Plastics: linear and cross-linked arrangements.
Thermoplastics (Polythene, PVC) vs Thermosetting plastics (Bakelite, Melamine).
Plastics and Environment: non-biodegradable nature, 4R principle (Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Recover).
learning_outcomes: Distinguish between natural and synthetic fibres.
Compare thermoplastics and thermosetting plastics.
Adopt the 4R principle in daily plastic management.

activities.title: Testing the Tensile Strength of Different Fibres
activities.aim: To compare the tensile strength of cotton, wool, silk, and nylon threads of identical length and thickness.
apparatus: Threads of cotton, wool, silk, and nylon of equal length and thickness
procedure: Tie a 60 cm piece of cotton thread to the clamp so that it hangs freely.
Suspend a light pan at the free end and add weights one by one until the thread breaks.
Note the total weight required to break the thread.
Repeat the procedure with wool, silk, and nylon threads.
precautions: All threads must be of identical length and thickness.
Add weights gently without jerking.
activities.observations: Nylon thread requires the maximum weight to break, followed by silk, cotton, and wool.
activities.conclusion: Nylon possesses the highest tensile strength among the tested fibres.

theorems_and_key_concepts: Sound is produced by vibrating bodies.
In humans, sound is produced by the voice box or larynx; vocal cords vibrate when air passes.
Sound requires a material medium (solid, liquid, or gas) to travel; it cannot travel through vacuum.
Human ear structure: outer ear (pinna), ear canal, eardrum (tympanum), middle ear bones, inner ear (cochlea).
Characteristics of sound waves: Amplitude, Frequency, Time period.
Loudness is proportional to square of amplitude; Pitch (shrillness) is determined by frequency.
Audible range of human hearing: 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Infrasonic (< 20 Hz) and Ultrasonic (> 20 kHz).
Noise vs Music; Noise pollution, health hazards, and mitigation measures.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate that vibrating bodies produce sound.
Explain how sound propagates through solids, liquids, and gases.
Distinguish between loudness and pitch.

activities.title: Demonstrating that Sound Cannot Travel Through Vacuum
activities.aim: To show that a material medium is essential for the propagation of sound.
procedure: Suspend an electric bell inside an airtight glass bell jar connected to a vacuum pump.
Switch on the bell and listen to the clear ringing sound.
Start the vacuum pump to gradually evacuate air from the jar while the hammer keeps striking.
precautions: The bell jar base must be sealed airtight with grease.
The bell must hang freely without touching jar walls.
activities.observations: As air is pumped out, the sound of the bell becomes feebler and eventually fades into silence, even though the hammer is seen striking.
activities.conclusion: Sound requires a material medium to propagate and cannot travel through vacuum.

theorems_and_key_concepts: Physical properties of metals: Malleability, Ductility, Sonorousness, Lustre, Good conductivity of heat and electricity.
Physical properties of non-metals: Brittle, Dull appearance, Poor conductors (except graphite).
Chemical properties: Reaction with oxygen to form oxides (Metal oxides are basic; Non-metal oxides are acidic).
Reaction with water: Metals form hydroxides and hydrogen gas (Sodium reacts vigorously).
Reaction with acids: Active metals displace hydrogen gas with a pop sound.
Displacement reactions: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution.
Uses of metals and non-metals in machinery, fertilisers, water purification, crackers, and medicines.
learning_outcomes: Compare physical and chemical properties of metals and non-metals.
Demonstrate acidic nature of non-metal oxides and basic nature of metal oxides.
Predict displacement reactions using reactivity series.

activities.title: Displacement Reaction Between Iron and Copper Sulphate
activities.aim: To demonstrate that iron displaces copper from copper sulphate solution.
procedure: Clean two iron nails thoroughly with sandpaper.
Take 10 mL of blue copper sulphate solution in a test tube.
Immerse one iron nail into the solution and leave undisturbed for 20 minutes.
Compare the colour of the solution and the nail with the control set.
precautions: Clean iron nails to remove any surface rust or grease.
Handle copper sulphate carefully as it is toxic.
activities.observations: The blue colour of copper sulphate solution fades to light green (FeSO4), and a reddish-brown coating of copper deposits on the iron nail.
activities.conclusion: Iron, being more reactive than copper, displaces copper from copper sulphate solution.

theorems_and_key_concepts: Laws of Reflection: 1. Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection; 2. Incident ray, normal, and reflected ray lie in the same plane.
Regular and Diffuse reflection.
Characteristics of image formed by a plane mirror: Virtual, erect, laterally inverted, same size, equidistant.
Multiple reflections and Kaleidoscope: Number of images n = (360 / theta) - 1.
Dispersion of light: Splitting of white light into constituent colours (VIBGYOR) through a prism.
Structure of human eye: Cornea, Iris, Pupil, Lens, Retina (Rods and Cones), Blind spot.
Care of the eyes and Braille system for visually challenged persons.
learning_outcomes: Verify the laws of reflection experimentally.
Calculate the number of images formed by inclined plane mirrors.
Explain the structure of the human eye and mechanism of vision.
key_formulas_and_equations: n = \frac{360^\circ}{\theta} - 1 \quad (\text{Number of images between inclined mirrors})

activities.title: Verifying the Laws of Reflection of Light
activities.aim: To verify that angle of incidence equals angle of reflection on a plane mirror.
procedure: Fix a white paper on the drawing board and draw a line MM' to place the mirror vertically.
Draw a normal ON and an incident ray AO at an angle of 30 degrees.
Fix two pins P and Q vertically on the incident ray line.
Look at the images of P and Q in the mirror and fix two more pins R and S such that R, S and images of P, Q lie in a straight line.
Remove the mirror and pins, join RS to O to get reflected ray OB, and measure angle of reflection r.
precautions: Pins must be fixed vertically.
Mirror must be perfectly perpendicular to paper.
activities.observations: The measured angle of reflection r is found to be exactly equal to angle of incidence i (30 degrees).
activities.conclusion: The angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection, verifying the first law of reflection.

theorems_and_key_concepts: Liquids that conduct electricity: Solutions of acids, bases, and salts.
Pure distilled water is a poor conductor; adding salt makes it a good conductor.
Electrolysis: Chemical decomposition produced by passing electric current through a conducting liquid.
Electrolysis of water: Evolving Oxygen gas at anode (+) and Hydrogen gas at cathode (-).
Electroplating: The process of depositing a thin layer of any desired metal on another material by means of electricity.
Applications of electroplating: Chromium plating for lustre and scratch resistance, Gold/Silver plating on jewellery, Tin plating on cans, Zinc galvanisation on iron.
learning_outcomes: Test electrical conductivity of various liquids using an LED tester.
Explain electrolysis of water and identify products at electrodes.
Demonstrate copper electroplating on an iron object.

activities.title: Electroplating of Copper on an Iron Key
activities.aim: To deposit a uniform coating of copper on an iron key by electroplating.
procedure: Dissolve two teaspoonfuls of copper sulphate in 250 mL of distilled water in a beaker, and add a few drops of dilute sulphuric acid to enhance conductivity.
Clean a copper plate and an iron key with sandpaper.
Connect the copper plate to the positive terminal of the battery (anode) and the iron key to the negative terminal (cathode).
Immerse both electrodes in the copper sulphate solution and pass current for 15 minutes.
precautions: Clean electrodes thoroughly to remove oxide layers.
Do not allow electrodes to touch each other in the solution.
activities.observations: A reddish-brown, shiny layer of copper is deposited on the iron key.
activities.conclusion: Electric current causes copper ions from the solution to deposit on the negative cathode, while copper from the anode replenishes the solution (electroplating).

theorems_and_key_concepts: Charging by friction: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
Two types of electrical charges: Positive and Negative.
Gold-leaf electroscope: Device used to test whether an object is carrying electric charge.
Lightning: Giant electric discharge between oppositely charged clouds or between cloud and earth.
Lightning safety measures and Lightning conductors invented by Benjamin Franklin.
Earthquakes: Sudden shaking or trembling of the earth caused by disturbance deep inside Earth's crust (tectonic plates).
Richter scale (logarithmic magnitude scale) and Seismograph. Safety measures during earthquakes.
learning_outcomes: Construct an improvised electroscope using a glass jar and aluminium foil.
Explain the phenomenon of lightning and action of lightning conductors.
Describe precautions to be taken during an earthquake.
key_formulas_and_equations: \text{Each unit increase on Richter scale corresponds to } 30\text{-fold increase in energy}

activities.title: Making a Simple Electroscope
activities.aim: To construct a simple electroscope to detect electric charge.
apparatus: Empty jam bottle with plastic lid
Aluminium foil strips (4 cm x 1 cm each)
procedure: Make a hole in the plastic lid of the bottle and insert the unbent paper clip.
Hang two identical aluminium foil strips from the bottom hook of the paper clip.
Fit the lid tightly on the bottle.
Touch the top end of the paper clip with a charged plastic comb.
precautions: Ensure aluminium foil leaves are lightweight and clean.
Do not touch the leaves with bare hands to avoid discharge.
activities.observations: The two aluminium foil leaves diverge (spread apart) when touched by the charged comb.
activities.conclusion: Like charges transferred to both foil strips repel each other, confirming the presence of charge.

theorems_and_key_concepts: Combustion is a chemical process in which a substance reacts with oxygen to give off heat and light.
Combustible vs non-combustible substances.
Conditions necessary for combustion: Combustible substance, supporter of combustion (oxygen/air), and attainment of ignition temperature.
Ignition temperature is the lowest temperature at which a substance catches fire.
Inflammable substances have low ignition temperature (petrol, alcohol, LPG).
How we control fire: Fire extinguishers, role of carbon dioxide in smothering fire.
Types of combustion: Rapid combustion, Spontaneous combustion, Explosion.
Structure of flame: Dark inner zone, luminous middle zone, non-luminous outer zone (hottest).
Calorific value of fuel (kJ/kg) and harmful products of burning fuels (CO, CO2, SO2, acid rain).
learning_outcomes: Identify essential conditions for combustion.
Draw and label the three zones of a candle flame.
Calculate calorific value of fuels.

activities.title: Demonstration that Air (Oxygen) is Necessary for Combustion
activities.aim: To show that continuous supply of air is necessary for combustion of a candle.
procedure: Fix a lighted candle on a table and place a glass chimney over it resting on two wooden blocks so air can enter from below.
Now remove the blocks and let the chimney rest on the table (cutting off bottom air).
Finally, cover the top of the chimney with a glass plate.
precautions: Ensure the candle flame does not touch the sides of the chimney.
Perform carefully to avoid burns.
activities.observations: In case 1, the candle burns steadily. In case 2, the flame flickers and produces smoke. In case 3, the flame completely extinguishes.
activities.conclusion: Continuous supply of oxygen (air) is indispensable for combustion.

chapter_end_exercises.question_text_en: In an experiment, 4.5 kg of a fuel was completely burnt. The heat produced was measured to be 180,000 kJ. Calculate calorific value.
chapter_end_exercises.question_text_te: ఒక ప్రయోగంలో 4.5 కిలోగ్రాముల ఇంధనం సంపూర్ణంగా దహనం చెంది 180,000 kJ ఉష్ణశక్తిని విడుదల చేసింది. ఆ ఇంధన కెలోరిఫిక్ విలువను లెక్కించండి.

chapter_end_exercises.question_text_en: Draw a neat labeled diagram of a candle flame showing its three zones.
chapter_end_exercises.question_text_te: కొవ్వొత్తి జ్వాల యొక్క చక్కని పటం గీసి మూడు మండలాలను గుర్తించండి.

theorems_and_key_concepts: Celestial objects: Stars, planets, moons, asteroids, comets, meteors, and meteorites.
Moon: Phases of moon caused by changing visible illuminated portion; 29.5 days lunar cycle.
Stars: Giant balls of glowing gas emitting light through nuclear fusion; Sun is the nearest star.
Light year: Distance travelled by light in one year = 9.46 * 10^12 km.
Pole Star (Dhruva Tara): Situated in line with Earth's rotational axis, appears stationary.
Constellations: Recognisable patterns formed by groups of stars (Ursa Major/Great Bear, Orion, Cassiopeia).
The Solar System: Sun and eight revolving planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune).
Artificial satellites and their applications in communication, weather remote sensing, and navigation.
learning_outcomes: Explain the phases of the moon with a diagram.
Locate the Pole star with the help of Ursa Major constellation.
Describe the distinguishing features of the eight planets in the solar system.

activities.title: Locating the Pole Star using Ursa Major (Saptarshi)
activities.aim: To identify and locate the Pole Star in the northern night sky using the pointer stars of Ursa Major.
procedure: Look towards the northern part of the night sky during summer and spot the seven prominent stars of Ursa Major (Saptarshi).
Identify the two pointer stars at the end of the bowl of Ursa Major.
Imagine a straight line passing through these two pointer stars and extend it towards the north.
Look for a moderately bright star along this line.
precautions: Choose a clear night away from bright city streetlights.
Ensure you are facing true North.
activities.observations: A solitary star of moderate brightness shines steadily along the extension of the pointer stars.
activities.conclusion: The star located is the Pole Star (Polaris), which appears stationary because it lies along the rotational axis of Earth.

chapter_end_exercises.question_text_en: Explain why the Pole Star appears stationary in the night sky while other stars appear to move from east to west.
chapter_end_exercises.question_text_te: ఇతర నక్షత్రాలన్నీ తూర్పు నుండి పడమరకు కదులుతున్నట్లు కనిపించినప్పటికీ ధ్రువ నక్షత్రం నిశ్చలంగా ఎందుకు కనిపిస్తుందో వివరించండి.
